prompt: why is the ocean salty but rivers aren't
completion: Rivers do carry salt, just in amounts too small to taste. Rain is slightly acidic, and as it runs over rock it dissolves tiny quantities of minerals, sodium and chloride among them, and rivers deliver those to the sea. When seawater evaporates, the water rises but the salt stays behind. Repeat that for a few billion years and the dissolved minerals accumulate until roughly three and a half percent of seawater, by weight, is salt. A river is a conveyor belt; the ocean is where the conveyor ends.

prompt: how does a fridge keep stuff cold
completion: A refrigerator doesn't make cold; it moves heat out of the box and dumps it into your kitchen. It does this with a fluid that boils at a very low temperature. Inside the fridge, the fluid evaporates in a set of coils, and evaporation absorbs heat, the same reason a wet arm feels cool in a breeze. A compressor then squeezes the warm vapor, raising its temperature, and pumps it to coils on the back or underside, where it releases that heat into the room and condenses back into a liquid. The liquid returns inside to evaporate again, and the cycle repeats. If you've ever felt warm air near the bottom of a fridge, you were feeling the heat it had carried out of your groceries.

prompt: how do earthquakes happen
completion: The Earth's outer shell is broken into enormous plates that drift a few centimeters a year. Where plates meet, they often lock together at their edges while the rest keeps moving, and the rock along the boundary bends and stores strain, like a stick slowly flexed between your hands. Eventually the strain exceeds what the rock can bear, and it slips suddenly along a fault. The stored energy radiates outward as waves through the ground, and those waves are what we feel as an earthquake.

prompt: how does gps know where i am
completion: About thirty satellites orbit the Earth, each carrying an extremely accurate atomic clock and continuously broadcasting its position and the exact time. Your phone listens for these signals. Because radio travels at the speed of light, the tiny delay between when a signal was sent and when it arrived tells your phone how far away that satellite is. Knowing your distance from one satellite places you somewhere on a sphere; with four or more, those spheres intersect at a single point, and that point is you. The satellites never learn where you are; your phone does all the calculating.

prompt: what's the difference between a president and a prime minister
completion: Both lead governments, but they get their power differently. A president in a system like the United States' is elected separately from the legislature and serves a fixed term, so the executive and the lawmakers can be controlled by opposing parties. A prime minister is typically the leader of whichever party or coalition commands a majority in parliament, and stays in office only as long as that support holds. Many countries have both: a ceremonial president or monarch as head of state, and a prime minister who actually runs the government.

prompt: what's the difference between a virus and bacteria
completion: Bacteria are living single-celled organisms. They eat, grow, and reproduce on their own, and most are harmless or even helpful; your gut alone houses trillions of them. Viruses are much smaller and far stranger: little more than genetic instructions wrapped in a protein coat, with no machinery to reproduce on their own. To multiply, a virus has to enter a living cell and hijack it into making copies. The difference matters for treatment. Antibiotics attack structures that bacteria have and our cells lack, so they're useless against viruses, which is why they won't help with a cold or the flu.

prompt: how do i make friends after moving to a new city
completion: Friendship mostly grows out of repeated, low-stakes contact, so the trick is to put yourself somewhere you'll see the same people again and again. A weekly class, a running club, a choir, a volunteer shift, or a recreational sports team will do more than any number of one-off events, because the second and third meetings are where acquaintances start to become friends. When you click with someone, be the one who suggests a specific plan: coffee on Thursday, not "we should hang out sometime." It will feel forward. Almost everyone is quietly relieved when someone else makes the first move.

prompt: how should i prepare for a job interview
completion: Study the company enough to say, in your own words, what it does and why the role interests you. Then reread the job description and, for each major requirement, prepare a short story from your experience that shows you doing that thing: the situation, what you did, and how it turned out. Rehearse those stories aloud until they're crisp but not memorized. Prepare two or three thoughtful questions of your own, since an interview is also your chance to judge them. Finally, handle the logistics the day before, such as the route, the link, and the outfit, so that your attention on the day goes to the conversation.

prompt: how do i take better photos with my phone
completion: Pay attention to light before anything else. Soft light, such as overcast skies, the hour after sunrise or before sunset, or a window beside your subject, flatters almost everything, while harsh midday sun creates hard shadows and squinting faces. Wipe the lens; a fingerprint smudge is behind more blurry photos than any shaky hand. Get closer than feels natural, and keep the background simple. Before you press the shutter, tap the screen to focus on your subject and drag the exposure slider down slightly, since phones tend to brighten scenes too much. And take several shots, then keep only the best one.

prompt: i have a presentation tomorrow and i'm super nervous
completion: Nerves before a presentation are almost universal, and they show far less from the outside than they feel from the inside. Tonight, run through the talk out loud once or twice, standing up, paying special attention to your first minute; a confident start carries momentum into everything after it. Then stop rehearsing and get some sleep. Tomorrow, before you begin, take a few slow breaths, with the exhale longer than the inhale, which genuinely calms the body. And remember that your audience wants you to do well. They're not waiting for a mistake; they're waiting to learn something.

prompt: a coworker keeps taking credit for my work. what should i do
completion: Start by making your work visible in ways that don't depend on anyone else's honesty. Share progress in group channels and meetings, send brief summary emails after you finish something, and present your own work whenever you can. If it keeps happening, talk to the coworker directly and calmly: "In the meeting, the analysis was described as yours. I did most of that work, and I'd like us to be clear about who did what." Sometimes that's enough. If it continues, bring specifics to your manager, focusing on the facts and the effect on your work rather than on the other person's motives. A paper trail makes that conversation much easier.

prompt: how do i set boundaries with my boss who messages me late at night
completion: Set the boundary through behavior first, then words if needed. Unless something is truly urgent, wait until the morning to reply, and do it promptly and well when you do. Most managers adjust quickly once they see that night messages get morning answers without any drop in quality. If it continues, raise it directly and frame it around doing good work: "I've found I do my best work when I fully switch off in the evenings. Unless something's urgent, is it all right if I respond to late messages first thing in the morning?" Asking what counts as urgent also helps, because it gives both of you a shared line to work with.

prompt: should i learn python or javascript first
completion: Choose by what you want to build. If you're drawn to websites and things people can click on, start with JavaScript, since it runs in every browser and you'll see your results immediately. If you're more interested in data, automation, scientific work, or general programming, start with Python, whose syntax is famously clean and close to plain English, which makes it a gentle first language. Either way, the important skills transfer: thinking in steps, breaking problems down, reading errors calmly. Your second language will come much faster than your first.

prompt: kindle or paper books
completion: Both, if you can, because they're good at different things. A Kindle is unbeatable for travel, for reading in bed with the lights off, for adjusting the type size, and for getting a book the moment you want it. Paper is better for books you'll flip back through, for anything with maps, diagrams, or photographs, and for the quiet pleasure of a shelf that remembers what you've read. If you have to choose one, ask where you do most of your reading. For commuters and travelers, the e-reader wins; for people who read at home and like to lend books, paper does.

prompt: what's a good first car
completion: Something reliable, safe, inexpensive to insure, and dull enough that you'll never be tempted to drive it like a race car. A used compact sedan or hatchback from a brand known for reliability, a few years old, with a documented maintenance history, is usually the sensible choice. Check the safety ratings, have an independent mechanic inspect it before you buy, and compare insurance quotes, since they vary enormously between models. Your first car's job is to get you everywhere safely without draining your bank account, and the ones that do that best are rarely the exciting ones.

prompt: write a bedtime story about a sleepy dragon
completion: In the high mountains, where the clouds sleep on the peaks, there lived a dragon named Ember who was very, very bad at staying awake. Other dragons guarded their gold all night with blazing eyes. Ember tried. She curled around her small pile of coins and buttons, which was mostly buttons, and she watched the cave entrance with great determination. But the stars came out one by one, and the wind hummed through the rocks like someone singing low, and her eyelids grew as heavy as anvils. "Just a little rest," she said, and laid her chin on her tail. Her breath slowed to a warm, gentle puff, puff, puff, and each puff made a tiny orange glow that lit the cave like a nightlight. Down in the valley, the village children saw the soft light flickering high on the mountain and felt safe, because they knew that up there, Ember was dreaming. And now it's time for you to dream too.

prompt: write a short fable about a fox and a crow, but with a twist
completion:
A crow sat in a tree with a piece of cheese, and a fox came by and began to flatter her. "What glossy feathers," said the fox. "What a graceful neck. Surely a bird so beautiful must have a voice to match." The crow had heard this story before, as all crows have. She put the cheese carefully under her foot and said, "Thank you. You have a lovely voice yourself. Won't you sing for me?" The fox, who had never been asked, was so pleased that he threw back his head and howled a long, quavering note. The crow listened politely until he finished. Then she ate the cheese, and the fox went home hungry but strangely happy, and he came back the next day to sing again.

Moral: Flattery works on everyone, including the flatterer.

prompt: write a gracious resignation letter
completion:
Dear Ms. Alvarez,

Please accept this letter as formal notice of my resignation from my position as project coordinator. My last day will be Friday, March 14, two weeks from today.

This was not an easy decision. I've learned a great deal here over the past three years, and much of that is thanks to your guidance and the trust you've placed in me. I'm especially grateful for the chance to lead the regional rollout, which taught me more than any job I've had.

I'll do everything I can to make the transition smooth, including documenting my current projects and helping to train whoever takes them on. Please let me know how I can best help in the coming weeks.

Thank you again for everything. I hope our paths cross again.

Sincerely,
Jordan Lee

prompt: tighten this up: In my personal opinion, I think that we should probably consider the possibility of maybe changing the plan.
completion:
"I think we should change the plan."

The original hedges six times: "in my personal opinion," "I think," "probably," "consider," "the possibility of," and "maybe." One hedge is enough to show you're offering a view rather than a command. If you want to soften it further, try "I'd suggest we change the plan."

prompt: rewrite this sentence with stronger verbs: She went quickly across the room and put the book down on the table.
completion:
"She crossed the room and dropped the book on the table."

Or, depending on her mood: "She strode across the room and slapped the book onto the table." A precise verb carries both the action and its manner, so it can replace a weaker verb plus an adverb. "Went quickly" becomes "strode" or "hurried"; "put down" becomes "dropped" or "set," which tell us different things about her.

prompt: fewer or less? i always mix them up
completion: Use "fewer" for things you can count individually, and "less" for things you measure as an amount. "Fewer cookies, fewer people, fewer mistakes," but "less sugar, less time, less patience." The test is whether you could put a number in front of the noun: you can have three cookies, but not three sugars. The supermarket sign that says "10 items or less" is technically wrong, though it's so common that almost nobody minds.

prompt: could a person outrun a t rex
completion: It's genuinely uncertain, which makes it a fun question. Estimates of Tyrannosaurus rex's top speed have varied widely, from around 10 to 25 miles per hour, and some researchers argue that its sheer weight would have limited it to a fast walk, since its leg bones might not have survived a true sprint. A fit human sprinter can reach over 20 miles per hour briefly, while most of us top out somewhere around 15. So an Olympic sprinter might win a short race, and the rest of us would be gambling. The best strategy, as with most large predators, would be not to be noticed in the first place.

prompt: is water wet
completion: It depends on what you mean by "wet." If wetness is the state of having water on you, then water isn't wet in the way that a towel or a dog can be; it's the thing doing the wetting. On the other hand, a drop of water is surrounded by other water, and if we define "wet" as being covered in liquid, then water is about as wet as anything can be. Scientists tend to describe wetting as how well a liquid spreads over a solid surface, which leaves water out of the category entirely. It's a good example of how a word that feels simple turns slippery the moment you look closely, which, under the circumstances, seems appropriate.

prompt: why do people like scary movies
completion: Because they let us feel fear without being in danger, and that turns out to be a surprisingly pleasant combination. A frightening scene sets off the body's alarm system: your heart races, your muscles tense, adrenaline floods in. But part of your mind knows you're safe on a sofa, so the experience becomes a thrill rather than a threat, and the relief afterward feels good. Scary movies also let us rehearse fear, imagining how we'd cope with danger, and they bring people together: there's real closeness in grabbing someone's arm in the dark and then laughing at yourself when the cat jumps out of the cupboard.

prompt: good morning
completion: Good morning. I hope the coffee is strong and the day is kind. What can I help you with?

prompt: how long should i steep green tea
completion: Two to three minutes, in water around 80 degrees Celsius, well below boiling. Green tea turns bitter when it's steeped too long or too hot, so err on the short side and taste as you go.

prompt: i'm tired
completion: Then rest if you can, even for twenty minutes. If you can't, a glass of water and a few minutes of daylight help more than you'd expect. Is it the sleepy kind of tired or the worn-down kind?

prompt: why is my computer so slow
completion: The most common causes are surprisingly ordinary. Too many programs running at once, especially browsers with dozens of tabs, can fill up your memory, forcing the computer to shuffle data back and forth to storage. A nearly full hard drive slows things down too. Programs that launch themselves at startup and run quietly in the background add up over time. And older computers with spinning hard drives rather than solid-state drives are much slower to load anything. A good first step is to open your task manager, called Activity Monitor on a Mac, and see what's using the most memory and processor time. Restarting occasionally also clears out a surprising amount of accumulated clutter.

prompt: should i specialize or be a generalist
completion: Early in a career, breadth tends to pay off: you learn how different parts of a system fit together, discover what you enjoy, and become adaptable. Over time, most people benefit from developing real depth in one or two areas, because deep expertise is rarer and harder to replace. A common and effective shape is to be broadly competent across your field and genuinely excellent in one corner of it. Choose that corner by what you find yourself curious about even when nobody's asking, since that curiosity is what sustains the long, unglamorous work of becoming an expert.

prompt: explain dns simply
completion: DNS, the Domain Name System, is the internet's phone book. Computers find each other using numerical addresses, like 93.184.216.34, but people prefer names like example.com. When you type a name into your browser, your computer asks a DNS server what number belongs to that name. If that server doesn't know, it asks others, working down from the servers responsible for ".com" to the ones responsible for that specific domain, until it gets an answer. The result is cached along the way, so the next lookup is faster. All of this usually takes a few milliseconds, before the page even begins to load.
